paper.citation: Lutz C, Mancino F, Parker DA. 12-Months MRI after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Can Identify Risk Factors for Subsequent Graft Rupture and Used to Guide the Return to Sport. Results From a High-Volume Institution. Journal of ISAKOS. 2025.
paper.abstract: Retrospective matched comparison of 13 patients with early hamstring-autograft ACL re-rupture and 50 matched controls, drawn from 430 primary ACL reconstructions (2017 to 2022) at one high-volume institution. Mean follow-up was 23.6 months. Re-rupture patients had higher graft signal on 12-month MRI (SNQ 2.93 vs 2.02, p=0.029). Tunnel position and widening, patient-reported outcomes and return-to-sport tests did not differ significantly between groups.
paper.tldr: In this small single-centre matched comparison, a higher signal on 12-month MRI after hamstring ACL reconstruction was seen in patients who later re-tore their graft. Return-to-sport tests did not separate the groups, and the multivariable model did not confirm graft signal, so this is a hypothesis to test rather than a clearance rule.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of 430 consecutive skeletally mature patients with primary hamstring-autograft ACLR. Of 346 meeting criteria, 19 ruptured and 13 with complete 12-month MRI formed the re-tear group, matched 1:4 to 50 controls. Graft signal (signal-to-noise quotient), tunnel widening and tunnel position were measured on 3.0-T MRI, with side-to-side laxity (GnRB) and return-to-sport tests at 9 to 12 months.
paper.findings: Re-tear patients had a higher mean 12-month SNQ (2.93 vs 2.02, p=0.029; Cohen's d 0.44), and 69.2% had SNQ above 2 vs 38% of controls (p=0.044). Anterior laxity above 2 mm was more frequent in the re-tear group (83.3% vs 38.8%, p=0.058), but mean laxity did not differ significantly (2.5 vs 1.3 mm, p=0.189). Femoral tunnel widening above 50% was actually more common in controls (36% vs 7.7%, p=0.155), and logistic regression did not identify graft signal, tunnel widening or laxity as significant risk factors (R2N=0.28).
paper.limitations: Only 13 re-tears were analysed, and 6 of 19 ruptures were excluded for missing 12-month MRI, which the authors flag as a possible detection bias. The design is retrospective, different assessors measured clinical, laxity and return-to-sport outcomes, and the cohort used one graft and fixation type in adults not described as athletes. The regression did not confirm graft signal (p=0.244), and the discussion gives 38.8% for control SNQ above 2 where Table 2 gives 38%.
paper.practicalImplications: A high 12-month graft signal was more common in patients who re-tore, so it may justify closer follow-up or repeat imaging before a full return to sport for higher-risk patients. The study does not establish a cut-off that should delay clearance, and the multivariable model did not confirm graft signal as an independent risk factor.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not measure training or performance outcomes. Its performance-relevant result is that hop, leg-length and ACL-RSI results at 9 to 12 months did not differ between re-tear and non-re-tear patients, so test scores in this cohort did not identify who would re-tear.
paper.rtp: The study can inform the monitoring discussion but not a clearance threshold. High 12-month graft signal was associated with early re-tear in a small matched comparison, and the authors suggest repeat MRI may inform return-to-sport decisions. It should not set a return-to-sport date, because return-to-sport tests did not predict re-rupture and the multivariable model did not confirm graft signal.

records.sourceFile: 3-Dimensional biomechanics of noncontact anterior cruciate ligament injuries in male professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Zago M, Esposito F, Stillavato S, Zaffagnini S, Frigo CA, Della Villa F. 3-Dimensional Biomechanics of Noncontact Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Male Professional Soccer Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024:1-10.
paper.abstract: Video analysis of 33 male professional soccer ACL injuries (24 noncontact, 9 indirect contact) from the 2020-2021 to 2022-2023 seasons, with 3D whole-body kinematics reconstructed by model-based image matching. At the injury frame, the knee was moderately flexed with a valgus trend and external rotation, and the hip was flexed, abducted and slightly internally rotated. Knee kinematics were consistent across situational patterns, while ankle, hip and trunk differed. The authors conclude that injury biomechanics vary with the game situation.
paper.tldr: Reconstructed 3D video analysis of 33 professional male soccer ACL injuries shows a moderately flexed knee with a valgus trend and rapid rotation changes before the injury frame. Ankle, hip and trunk postures differed by game situation, but the study does not test any prevention intervention.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional video analysis of ACL injuries in 6 national and 2 international competitions, using publicly available broadcast footage. Of 47 identified injuries, 33 had suitable multi-view video. Model-based image matching reconstructed 3D joint angles from 400 ms before to 200 ms after the injury frame, and situational patterns were compared with one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping ANOVA.
paper.findings: Across 33 injuries, mean knee flexion at the injury frame was 45.9 ± 21.7 degrees, with 4.3 ± 5.1 degrees of abduction and 3.0 ± 6.4 degrees of external rotation, while the hip was flexed 32.0 ± 18.7 degrees, abducted 31.1 ± 12.0 degrees and slightly internally rotated (Table 1). A dynamic knee valgus pattern was seen in 22 of 33 cases (67%), and the knee rotated externally by up to 5 degrees and then internally before the injury frame. The knee time course did not differ between pressing, offensive change-of-direction and regaining-balance patterns before 0.1 s after initial contact, whereas ankle, hip and trunk differences were significant.
paper.limitations: Only 33 of 47 identified injuries had video suitable for analysis, and the abstract's description of 33 consecutive cases should be read with that subset in mind. Injury timing was estimated from video, the model fixes tibiofemoral translations, and the method gives estimates rather than measurements. There was no uninjured control group, and the unequal situational groups (pressing 54% of noncontact cases) limit statistical power.
paper.practicalImplications: Because the knee pattern was similar across situations but hip, trunk and ankle postures differed, drills for pressing, change of direction and landing could be built to resemble those game situations. The authors' proposal to shift from general strengthening toward discipline-specific training is their recommendation and was not tested in this study.
paper.athleteDev: The study suggests that sidestepping, pressing and landing work should be representative of game situations, because the postures at injury varied with the situation. It does not test any training programme or show that changing these postures reduces injury.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes how noncontact ACL injuries occurred and does not assess rehabilitation progress, readiness tests or clearance criteria.

paper.citation: Kim S, Kleimeyer JP, Ahmed MA, Avins AL, Fredericson M, Dragoo JL, et al. A Genetic Marker Associated with Shoulder Dislocation. Int J Sports Med. 2017;38:508-514.
paper.abstract: Genome-wide association screen for shoulder dislocation using genotype and electronic health record data from the GERA cohort of Kaiser Permanente Northern California, including 662 cases and 82,602 controls of European ancestry. rs12913965, in an intron of the TICRR gene and associated with expression of ISG20, was associated with shoulder dislocation at genome-wide significance (p = 9.7 × 10^-9, OR 1.6). Carriers of one risk allele had a 69% higher risk of shoulder dislocation in this cohort, and the authors call for replication.
paper.tldr: In a large general-population genetic cohort, one variant (rs12913965) was associated with a higher rate of coded shoulder dislocation or stabilisation surgery. It has not been replicated or tested in athletes, so it is not ready for athlete screening.
paper.methods: Case-control genome-wide association study in the GERA cohort (n = 102,979), with the European-ancestry group (83,264 people) as the primary analysis. Cases were defined by ICD-9 codes for closed anterior, posterior or inferior shoulder dislocation or by CPT codes for capsulorrhaphy, and about 8 million genotyped and imputed SNPs were tested with logistic regression adjusted for sex, age at enrolment, ancestry principal components and genotyping variables. Genome-wide significance was set at p < 5 × 10^-8, with sex-specific analyses and fixed-effects meta-analyses with Latino and East Asian groups.
paper.findings: rs12913965 was the only genome-wide significant variant (additive OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.88; dominant OR 1.72, p = 3.6 × 10^-9; recessive model not significant, p = 0.146). Heterozygous carriers had a relative risk of 1.69 (95% CI 1.41 to 2.03) compared with non-carriers, while the 10 homozygous cases gave a non-significant relative risk of 1.61. The sex-specific odds ratios did not differ significantly, and the variant was not associated in the Latino (p = 0.9) or East Asian (p = 0.64) groups, so the EUR plus Latino meta-analysis (p = 5.5 × 10^-8) was driven by the European data.
paper.limitations: Phenotypes came from electronic health record codes, which the authors note may be inaccurate, and recurrent dislocations and multidirectional instability were excluded. The cohort was not selected for sport, and the association has not been replicated. The text gives 626 European cases in the methods but 662 elsewhere, and gives a risk allele frequency of 13% in the text but 0.10 in controls in Table 3.
paper.practicalImplications: This variant should not be used to screen or counsel athletes about shoulder dislocation risk, because it comes from one unreplicated general-population association. The authors' suggestion that it might one day identify athletes at higher risk is a hypothesis for future athlete studies.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure training or performance and does not include athlete data. It cannot inform training decisions.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after shoulder dislocation. It does not examine treatment, recurrence after return, or readiness criteria, and recurrent dislocations were excluded from the case definition.

paper.citation: Lamplot JD, Rodeo SA, Brophy RH. A practical guide for the current use of biologic therapies in sports medicine. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019:1-15.
paper.abstract: This Current Concepts review gives sports medicine clinicians a practical guide to biologic therapies, mainly PRP and BMAC. It covers FDA regulation, cost and insurance coverage, direct-to-consumer marketing, preparation variability, and clinical evidence for tendon, rotator cuff, ligament, cartilage and osteoarthritis indications. The authors conclude that these therapies remain at a proof-of-concept stage and need better-reported preparations and trials.
paper.tldr: Biologic injections such as PRP and BMAC are widely used in sports medicine, but this review finds their efficacy, cost-effectiveness and preparation are not well established. Clinicians should check the evidence for each indication and what the patient will pay.
paper.methods: Narrative review of FDA regulatory guidance, cost and insurance reports, direct-to-consumer marketing studies, and clinical studies and systematic reviews for each indication. A September 2018 ClinicalTrials.gov search was used to estimate the number of trials per indication. No formal systematic search or risk-of-bias method is described.
paper.findings: The FDA does not regulate point-of-care PRP or BMAC, but clinicians must register their use, and most insurers treat these therapies as experimental. Reported patient prices were a mean of $714 per same-day unilateral PRP knee injection (153 clinics) and $5156 per stem-cell knee injection (65 centers). The authors conclude there is a lack of evidence to support PRP augmentation of rotator cuff repair; for knee osteoarthritis several RCTs favored leukocyte-poor PRP over placebo or hyaluronic acid, although AAOS and NICE guidance calls the evidence inconclusive; and for ACL reconstruction, 6 of 11 RCTs reported faster graft maturation with PRP but only 1 reported better clinical outcomes.
paper.limitations: The authors note that most published studies lack enough detail on preparation to be reproduced, and that only 10% of PRP trials in orthopaedics gave a full protocol. The cartilage evidence rests on case series and small cohorts, and BMAC preparations vary widely in cell content, so dose and timing cannot be compared across studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Before recommending a biologic injection, clinicians should check the evidence for that specific indication, the patient's out-of-pocket cost, and the preparation's reported composition. Marketing claims cited in the review, such as satisfaction rates of 76% and efficacy of 82.2%, come from business-reported data and should not be used as evidence of benefit.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not evaluate biologic therapies for performance enhancement or training outcomes, so it cannot inform performance decisions. It is relevant when staff are asked to support an athlete's injection, where cost and evidence gaps should be explained.
paper.rtp: The review gives no return-to-sport timelines or clearance criteria. Its ACL findings show faster graft maturation with PRP in some trials, but only 1 of 11 RCTs reported better clinical outcomes, so it cannot be used to shorten return-to-sport timelines.

records.sourceFile: A Preventive Model For Hamstring Injuries in Professional Soccer- Learning Algorithms.pdf

paper.citation: Ayala F, López-Valenciano A, Gámez Martín JA, De Ste Croix M, Vera-Garcia FJ, García-Vaquero MP, et al. A preventive model for hamstring injuries in professional soccer: learning algorithms. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: This study compared machine-learning methods to find the best pre-season model for identifying professional soccer players at high risk of hamstring strain injury. Ninety-six male players from Spanish first and second B divisions completed personal, psychological and neuromuscular testing, and 18 hamstring injuries were recorded in the 2013/2014 season. The best model, a cost-sensitive ADTree ensemble, had an AUC of 0.837, a true positive rate of 77.8% and a true negative rate of 83.8% under cross-validation.
paper.tldr: A 66-measure pre-season screening model flagged hamstring injury risk in 96 Spanish professional soccer players with moderate-to-high accuracy in cross-validation. Its complexity and its basis in 18 injuries mean it needs external validation before it is used as a screening tool.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort in which 229 personal, psychological (sleep and burnout questionnaires) and neuromuscular measures (postural control, hip adduction and abduction strength, joint range of motion, core stability, isokinetic hamstring and quadriceps strength) were recorded before the season. Hamstring injuries were confirmed by club medical staff and followed for 9 months, and cost-sensitive, oversampling and ensemble methods with J48, ADTree and SimpleCart base classifiers were compared using 3-fold stratified cross-validation.
paper.findings: The best model reached an AUC of 0.837, a true positive rate of 77.8% (14 of 18 injuries detected) and a true negative rate of 83.8% (57 of 68 uninjured players), with 82.6% of instances correctly classified. Of 229 measures, 66 remained in the final model; sleep quality appeared in 5 of 10 classifiers, hip flexion range of motion with the knee extended in 4, and angle-specific isokinetic torque variables made up 45 of the 66 features.
paper.limitations: The 86 analysed players are 96 enrolled minus 6 who did not finish all neuromuscular tests and 4 who left their teams, a step described only in the supplement (SDC 8), and the team counts printed in the methods (25 and 73) sum to 98, not 96. Model selection, the cost matrix (false negative cost 11) and the reported accuracy all come from the same cross-validation folds, with no independent test set, and the claim that the AUC is significantly higher than earlier models is not tested statistically. Findings apply to male professional players in one season with 18 injuries.
paper.practicalImplications: The screening battery could help staff choose players for closer monitoring before the season, but the model needs external validation in another squad before its flags guide decisions. The factors it identifies, including sleep quality, burnout and angle-specific hamstring strength and range of motion, are hypotheses to check rather than validated cut-offs.
paper.athleteDev: Sleep quality was the most consistent variable across classifiers, so staff who already collect sleep and burnout questionnaires have a candidate risk marker to track, not a validated predictor. The full 66-measure battery is impractical for routine use, and the study does not show that acting on the flags reduces injuries.
paper.rtp: The study addresses pre-season prevention, not return to sport, and it gives no return-to-play criteria. A history of hamstring injury last season appeared in 3 of the 10 classifiers, but this does not establish how to manage a player returning from injury.

records.sourceFile: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Prevention Programs - Training to Stay in the Game.pdf

paper.citation: Watson SL, Gohal C, Owen MM, Bajaj PM, Plantz MA, Tjong VK. A systematic review and meta-analysis of anterior cruciate ligament injury prevention programs: training to stay in the game. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026.
paper.abstract: The authors pooled 18 studies of ACL injury prevention programs (9 randomized controlled trials and 9 prospective cohorts) in 25,166 mostly female athletes from handball, soccer, basketball and volleyball. Athletes in prevention programs had a pooled risk ratio of 0.46 for ACL rupture (95% CI 0.36 to 0.57), with significant reductions in every subgroup analysed. The authors conclude that neuromuscular training provides strong support for reducing ACL rupture risk.
paper.tldr: Neuromuscular training programs roughly halved ACL rupture rates in this pooled analysis of 18 studies, with the largest effect in soccer. The evidence comes mainly from female team-sport athletes, so the result should not be assumed for other groups.
paper.methods: Embase, PubMed and MEDLINE (Ovid) were searched without a PROSPERO registration, and two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently; two more studies were added from reference lists. Inverse-variance pooled risk ratios were calculated with restricted maximum-likelihood heterogeneity, a continuity correction of 0.5 for zero cells, and subgroup analyses where at least four studies reported the metric. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool for RCTs and MINORS for cohorts, and publication bias with a funnel plot and Egger test.
paper.findings: The pooled risk ratio for ACL rupture was 0.46 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.57; I2 49%), with absolute rates of 1.0% in intervention groups and 2.3% in controls. Risk reductions were significant for athletes under 18 (RR 0.35), 18 and older (RR 0.50), female athletes (RR 0.57, 12 studies), soccer (RR 0.30, 9 studies), handball (RR 0.66, 4 studies) and programs with balance boards (RR 0.49, 6 studies). The soccer estimate was lower than the handball estimate (Z test P=.0072).
paper.limitations: The authors note that the included athletes were mostly female, the interventions were team-based so the review cannot speak for individual athletes, the data focused on team sports, and it was hard to confirm that athletes had no prior musculoskeletal injury. Absolute ACL rupture rates were low, no male-only analysis was run because fewer than four studies reported it, and most studies followed athletes for one or two seasons (mean 1.3 seasons, excluding one 12-year study). The 2026 year is from the copyright line, as no issue date is printed.
paper.practicalImplications: Teams can add short neuromuscular training sessions (agility, speed, strength and landing or balance work) to regular practice, and the review supports balance-board work where possible. Delivery should be team-based, with coaches, strength staff and athletic trainers sharing the work, since the trials were team-based. Expect the soccer result to be strongest, and do not assume the same effect in handball, where the estimate was weaker.
paper.athleteDev: The authors note that these programs can enhance athletic performance, citing work outside this review, but this review did not measure performance. The included programs averaged about 18 minutes per session and fit into regular practice, which makes them practical for training plans.
paper.rtp: The review excluded studies of rehabilitation or reinjury after ACL reconstruction and studies of ACL-deficient knees, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its included studies are prevention trials and cohorts, not studies of athletes with an ACL-deficient knee.

records.sourceFile: A new conceptual framework for managing hamstring injury risk in soccer–implementing a data-informed approach - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Pillitteri G, Clemente FM, Petrucci M, Sarmento H, Figueiredo A, Bongiovanni T, et al. A new conceptual framework for managing hamstring injury risk in soccer: implementing a data-informed approach. A narrative review. Biol Sport 2026;43:329-353.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarises non-contact injury research in soccer, focusing on risk factors and the training load-injury relationship. It describes conceptual injury frameworks and cognitive biases in attributing injury to training load, and proposes a multilevel framework for hamstring injury. The framework centres on acute mechanical load tissue exposure and muscle tolerance to load, and supports a data-informed rather than purely data-driven approach to load management.
paper.tldr: The authors argue that hamstring injury in soccer is multifactorial, so training load and sprinting should be managed with a data-informed approach rather than judged alone. They propose two concepts, acute mechanical load tissue exposure and muscle tolerance to load, but these are conceptual and untested in the review.
paper.methods: Narrative review, described as using a qualitative approach, that summarises the soccer injury literature and proposes a conceptual framework. No systematic search strategy or study-quality appraisal is described, and Tables 1 and 2 are illustrative examples from a microcycle rather than study data.
paper.findings: The review reports that hamstring strain is the most common non-contact injury in professional male soccer (12-14% of all injuries and 37% of muscle injuries), and that most hamstring injuries occur while sprinting above about 80% of maximum speed. It concludes that training load is implicated in injury but cannot be the sole cause, because no study has established a causal link between training load and injury. The authors propose AMLTE and MTTL as the factors to manage, and their framework is conceptual rather than tested.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative and does not describe how studies were selected, so the evidence base cannot be checked. The authors acknowledge that randomised trials of training load and injury are scarce, and AMLTE and MTTL have no validated measures (the abstract calls the second concept CMTTL, the body mostly MTTL). The tables use hypothetical players, and the 1.8 training-to-match ratio labelled 'prepared' echoes a cited average training-to-match effort ratio but is not validated as an injury-risk threshold.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should use sprint and high-speed running data as one input alongside fitness, fatigue and readiness data, not as a sole predictor of injury. Players with low match-equivalent sprint exposure, such as non-starters, may need planned sprint work, and the authors give linear sprints of at least 40-50 m at maximal effort as an example. Training-to-match ratios can prompt review of a player's load, but the review's examples are illustrative and not validated thresholds.
paper.athleteDev: The framework supports planning sprint and high-speed exposure within the weekly microcycle, with compensatory sprint work for players who have low match exposure. The review cites Buchheit and colleagues for sprint exposure above 95% of maximum speed on MD-2 possibly being associated with lower injury rates, but the authors present the framework as conceptual rather than a proven performance method.
paper.rtp: The review addresses return to play only indirectly. It states that medical staff should confirm a player's tissues can withstand maximum effort before declaring them fit for a match, but it gives no validated return-to-play criteria. The authors also note that existing hamstring measures have minimal utility for predicting hamstring injury.

records.sourceFile: A preliminary study of the effectiveness of an   allostatic closed loop acoustic stimulation neurotechnology in the   treatment of athletes with persisting post concussion   symptoms.pdf

paper.citation: Tegeler CH, Tegeler CL, Cook JF, Lee SW, Gerdes L, Shaltout HA, et al. A preliminary study of the effectiveness of an allostatic, closed-loop, acoustic stimulation neurotechnology in the treatment of athletes with persisting post-concussion symptoms. Sports Medicine - Open. 2016;2:39.
paper.abstract: Open-label, single-site case series of 15 athletes with persisting post-concussion symptoms who received HIRREM, an allostatic, closed-loop acoustic stimulation neurotechnology. The authors report improved symptom questionnaire scores, some autonomic cardiovascular measures and drop-stick reaction time after treatment, and return to full sport participation in 10 of 15 athletes within 3 months. They conclude that a larger controlled trial is warranted.
paper.tldr: In this uncontrolled series of 15 athletes, symptom scores and some autonomic measures improved after HIRREM, and 10 of 15 returned to full sport participation. The design cannot separate the treatment from natural recovery or placebo, so treat it as a pilot signal for a controlled trial.
paper.methods: Open-label, single-site feasibility study; this report covers 15 athletes aged 14 to 23 who consented after screening. They received a mean of 18.7 HIRREM sessions over 29.6 days, with baseline and post-intervention measures of the RPQ, ISI, CES-D, short-term blood pressure and heart rate recordings for baroreflex sensitivity and HRV, and drop-stick reaction time in 7 athletes. Paired t tests were used, with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests as a non-parametric check.
paper.findings: Mean RPQ total fell by 19.7 points (SD 11.4; n = 12; Wilcoxon p = 0.001), with 14 of 16 items improved, and ISI (n = 15) and CES-D (n = 10) scores also fell. Several baroreflex sensitivity measures and SDNN increased significantly, but RMSSD, LF and HF power did not, and drop-stick distance fell from 23.8 to 19.8 cm (n = 7; Wilcoxon p = 0.016). All 15 returned to full exercise, and 10 returned to full sport participation, within 3 months of the post-HIRREM visit. The authors argue the pattern is not consistent with natural history or placebo, but no control group was tested.
paper.limitations: Without a control group, the changes cannot be attributed to HIRREM. Sample sizes differ by measure (n = 7 to 15), and self-reported outcomes are open to reporting bias. The placebo argument rests partly on comparing RPQ change with another trial's active and sham arms. Two co-authors are employees of Brain State Technologies, the device developer, and session counts (13 to 36) and months since concussion (0.5 to 11) varied widely.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use this study alone to justify HIRREM for athletes with persisting post-concussion symptoms. The results are a pilot signal that needs a controlled trial, because the single-arm design cannot separate the treatment from recovery over time. Any program that tries the approach should keep standard concussion evaluation and clearance in place.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure athletic performance or sport skill; the only performance-related measure is drop-stick reaction time, which improved in 7 athletes without a control group. It should not be used to support performance gains.
paper.rtp: The study cannot establish return-to-play readiness or clearance. Return to participation was recorded by follow-up questioning in an uncontrolled series with no graded return-to-play protocol or clearance criteria described; of the 5 who did not return to full sport, 2 college athletes were held out with persisting daily headaches and 3 chose not to return. The return rate should not be read as evidence that HIRREM speeds return to play.

paper.citation: Allahabadi S, Gatto AP, Pandya NK. ACL tears in the National Football League from 2013 to 2020: analysis of the 2020 season after delays and schedule changes from the early COVID-19 pandemic relative to prior seasons. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;10(2):23259671221076045.
paper.abstract: Publicly available data identified 379 ACL tears in NFL athletes from 2013 to 2020. Preseason injuries occurred at a higher rate per exposure than in-season injuries, and the proportion of in-season tears in 2020 was higher than in 2013 to 2018.
paper.tldr: In this descriptive NFL study, ACL tears were more frequent per exposure in the preseason, and the 2020 season (which had no preseason games) had more in-season tears. The data cannot show why.
paper.methods: Retrospective descriptive epidemiology study using publicly available records of ACL tears in active-roster NFL players from 2013 to 2020. Tears were classified as preseason or in-season and as practice or game, and rates were expressed per 1000 athlete-exposures. Chi-square, ANOVA and Tukey tests were used, with incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% CIs.
paper.findings: There were 379 tears: 256 (67.6%) in games and 118 (31.1%) in practice, with 182 (48.0%) preseason; practice tears were concentrated in the preseason (106 of 118, P < .0001). For 2013 to 2019, the preseason incidence rate was higher than in-season (IRR 2.67, 95% CI 2.15 to 3.33). In 2020, 78.6% of tears were in-season, higher than in each year from 2013 to 2018 (not 2019), and the 2020 in-season rate was reported as 1.49 times the 2014 to 2019 combined rate (95% CI 0.98 to 2.19; P = .048). September 2020 had 13 of 41 tears with a known month (31.7%), not significantly different from August's share in 2013 to 2019 (35.6%, P = .62).
paper.limitations: Exposure counted only active-roster games, so training camp and practice exposure is not captured, although practice tears are included in the counts; the data came from public sources and may miss tears. The abstract gives the preseason IRR as 2.68 (2.18 to 3.29) while the results give 2.67 (2.15 to 3.33). The 2020 in-season IRR (1.49) is called significant at P = .048 although its 95% CI (0.98 to 2.19) includes 1, and the Discussion reverses the results by stating an elevated total rate in 2020 versus 2014 to 2019 but no increased in-season rate.
paper.practicalImplications: Early-season planning should expect more tears in the first month of competitive play: August (the first preseason month) had the most tears in the pooled 2013 to 2019 data, and September had the most in 2020 when there was no preseason. Most practice-related tears occurred in the preseason (106 of 118), and the authors suggest gradually ramping up play minutes and keeping a focus on ACL prevention training early in competitive periods.
paper.athleteDev: Staff planning preseason and early-season load could expect higher tear counts in the first competitive month, as these NFL data showed. Snap counts and games played at injury did not differ by season, so this study does not show that fatigue measured by snaps drove the 2020 pattern.
paper.rtp: The study does not cover recovery or return to play after ACL reconstruction, so it cannot guide return timing for an injured player. It describes when tears occur in the season, not how long players need to return.
