paper.citation: Edwards S, Gardner AJ, Tahu T, Quarrie KL, Fuller GW, Strangman G, et al. A tackler correctly adhering to the tackle instruction in a front-on, one-on-one torso tackle alters the peak inertial head kinematics of the ball carrier but not the tackler. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: Fifteen male rugby players made front-on, one-on-one torso tackles under four instructions in a motion-capture lab. Adhering to the dominant torso and stick and smother pop and lock instructions increased the ball carrier's peak linear head acceleration, while adhering to the traditional smother instruction reduced it; the tackler's own head kinematics did not change significantly with adherence.
paper.tldr: In a lab study of 15 male rugby players, following the tackle instruction changed the ball carrier's peak head acceleration but not the tackler's. The study measured head kinematics, not concussion, so it does not show a change in injury risk.
paper.methods: Fifteen male rugby players (amateur, semi-professional and one international) each completed 40 tackles as tackler and 40 as ball carrier, across four instructions (two traditional NRL tackles and two novel variants) at 10 trials each. Trials were recorded with 300 Hz 3D motion capture, and two experts judged adherence. Mixed general linear models tested the effect of adherence on peak head kinematics and joint angles.
paper.findings: Of 594 trials analysed, 455 (77%) adhered to the instruction. Adherence did not significantly change the tackler's peak head kinematics. Ball carrier peak linear head acceleration was higher with adherence for the dominant torso and stick tackle (3.8 to 4.4 g) and smother pop and lock tackle (4.4 to 5.1 g), and lower for the traditional smother tackle (5.0 to 3.8 g), which also showed lower ball carrier peak angular acceleration. The dominant NRL tackle was adhered to in 99% of trials (Table 1).
paper.limitations: This was a preliminary study of one tackler against one ball carrier in a lab, with tackles not taken to ground, so it does not transfer to match play. The Discussion gives 46% non-adherence for the dominant torso and stick tackle and 53% and 65% adherence for the smother pop and lock and traditional smother tackles, while Table 1 gives 35% non-adherence for the dominant torso and stick tackle and 68% and 74% adherence for the two smother tackles; the record uses Table 1.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches teaching the dominant torso and stick or smother pop and lock tackles should know that correct execution raised the ball carrier's peak linear head acceleration in this lab, so these instructions are not shown to protect the ball carrier's head. When the smother pop and lock was performed correctly, tacklers showed more ankle dorsiflexion, pelvis flexion and lumbar flexion; when the dominant torso and stick was performed correctly, they showed less head and trunk flexion.
paper.athleteDev: For tackling skill work, staff can use the authors' cues: keep the gaze up and forward and avoid excess trunk flexion in the dominant torso and stick, and lower body height through the ankles and pelvis in the smother pop and lock. The study measured lab kinematics only, so these cues are not shown to lower injury risk.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to contact or recovery from concussion or any injury, so it cannot inform return-to-tackling decisions.

records.sourceFile: Acute adductor muscle injury - A systematic review on diagnostic imaging, treatment, and prevention.pdf

paper.citation: Farrell SG, Hatem M, Bharam S. Acute Adductor Muscle Injury: A Systematic Review on Diagnostic Imaging, Treatment, and Prevention. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023:1-13.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 30 studies (594 male athletes, mostly soccer) examined imaging, treatment and prevention of acute adductor injuries. Previous groin injury, adductor weakness, injury in the previous season and reduced rotational hip range were associated with acute adductor injury. Partial tears returned to play in 1 to 7 weeks with physical therapy, and nonoperative or surgical treatment was described as acceptable for complete adductor longus tears.
paper.tldr: Across 30 mostly observational studies in male athletes, mainly soccer players, complete adductor longus tears returned to play in about 9 weeks without surgery and 14 weeks after surgery, and partial tears in 1 to 7 weeks with physical therapy. The evidence that adductor strengthening prevents injury is mixed.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with PubMed and Web of Science searched to September 2021 for original studies of acute adductor injury in amateur or professional athletes (mean age over 15 years, evidence levels 1 to 4). Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts, one reviewer assessed full texts, and quality was rated with CONSORT-based scoring for trials and MINORS for observational studies. Averages were weighted by sample size, and no formal meta-analysis is reported.
paper.findings: On MRI, injuries involved the adductor longus in 92% of 296 patients, and complete tears were 21% to 25% of cases. For complete tears, mean return to play was 8.9 weeks with physical therapy (3 studies, 36 patients) and 14.2 weeks with surgery (3 studies, 26 patients), and the surgical groups had greater stump retraction and more severe injuries. Partial tears returned to play in 1 to 6.9 weeks depending on grade, and the pooled recurrence rate was 5% (range 0% to 19%). Risk factors were previous groin injury, adductor weakness, injury in the previous season and reduced rotational hip range, all from observational studies. The two randomized trials of adductor strengthening conflicted, as described in the evidence summary.
paper.limitations: The treatment section had no randomized trials, and 22 of 30 studies were level 4 observational studies, several with small numbers, such as 6 surgical patients in one study. Some studies share patients, the same lead author accounts for 47% of imaging and 30% of treatment studies, and the senior author (S.B.) declares fees from Smith & Nephew and authored an included surgical series. The two randomized prevention trials reported overall groin injuries, not acute adductor injuries specifically, and the nonoperative and surgical groups differed in injury severity, so the return-to-play difference cannot be attributed to treatment alone.
paper.practicalImplications: For complete adductor longus tears, the included studies used retraction thresholds (more than 1 cm or 2 cm) to choose surgery, but the evidence on retraction as a prognostic factor conflicts, so the return-to-play ranges are broad expectations rather than a guide to choosing treatment. Partial tears in these studies returned in 1 to 7 weeks with physical therapy. The authors suggest adductor strengthening may help athletes with previous groin injury or side-to-side weakness, but the randomized evidence on groin injury prevention conflicts.
paper.athleteDev: Observational studies link lower adductor strength and side-to-side asymmetry to later groin or adductor injury, which supports preseason adductor strength testing as a monitoring option. The randomized evidence for strengthening programs is mixed, so a program should not be assumed to prevent injuries.
paper.rtp: In these studies, partial tears returned to play in 1 to 7 weeks with physical therapy, and complete tears in about 9 weeks without surgery or 14 weeks with surgery. These are group averages from small series with different injury severity, so they are not individual return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Acute fatigue-induced alterations in hamstring muscle properties after repeated Nordic hamstring exercises.pdf

paper.citation: Podczarska-Glowacka M, Bogdanski B, Trybulski R, Smoter M, Wang HK, Klich S. Acute fatigue-induced alterations in hamstring muscle properties after repeated Nordic hamstring exercises. Science Progress. 2024;107(2):1-17.
paper.abstract: Twenty-two recreational active physiotherapy students completed six bouts of five Nordic hamstring exercise repetitions on a NordBord. Ultrasound, myotonometry, average force and RPE were measured at baseline, immediately after and 1 h after to track fatigue-related changes in the semitendinosus and biceps femoris long head.
paper.tldr: Six sets of five Nordic hamstring repetitions produced measurable short-term changes in hamstring thickness, pennation angle, fascicle length, stiffness and vascularity in recreational students. This single-session lab study does not show what those changes mean for injury risk.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures design with six bouts of five repetitions, 2 minutes passive rest between bouts. Outcomes were average force, RPE, myotonometer stiffness, B-mode ultrasound thickness, pennation angle and fascicle length, and power Doppler vascularity index for both muscles, analysed with one-way and two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: Average force fell and RPE rose across the bouts. Immediately after exercise, thickness and pennation angle increased, fascicle length decreased, stiffness rose (P = 0.005, pooled across muscles) and vascularity index increased in both muscles; by 1 h, thickness and pennation angle had decreased and fascicle length had increased. Stiffness was greater in the biceps femoris long head than the semitendinosus overall, and its vascularity index was greater than the semitendinosus at 1 h (p = 0.001).
paper.limitations: The sample was 22 physiotherapy students, 20 of them women, and the authors state the study should be repeated in athletes, split by sex, and that past injuries were not taken into account. The results text reports the vascularity increase only for immediately after exercise, while the abstract also reports one at 1 h. Several degrees of freedom do not match n = 22, some correlations are reported as r = 1.0, and no injury or performance outcomes were collected.
paper.practicalImplications: Within this single-session protocol, six sets of five repetitions produced fatigue (falling force, rising RPE) and short-term changes in hamstring architecture and vascularity. The authors propose that Nordic hamstring exercise could serve as a warm-up that also tracks strength, but this was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: The findings describe how a fatiguing Nordic hamstring protocol changes hamstring architecture and force output in the short term, which may inform how NHE sets are sequenced. They do not show a training adaptation, and no athletes were studied.
paper.rtp: The study cannot set return-to-sport criteria, since it included healthy recreational students with no injury and did not test whether the imaging or Doppler changes predict re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Additional evidence supports   association of common genetic variants in MMP3 and TIMP2 with increased   risk of chronic Achilles tendinopathy susceptibility.pdf

paper.citation: Nie G, Wen X, Liang X, Zhao H, Li Y, Lu J. Additional evidence supports association of common genetic variants in MMP3 and TIMP2 with increased risk of chronic Achilles tendinopathy susceptibility. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019.
paper.abstract: A genetic association study comparing 1,084 chronic Achilles tendinopathy patients with 2,188 controls, testing 21 tag SNPs in MMP3 and TIMP2. Two SNPs were associated with chronic tendinopathy risk, and one TIMP2 variant was linked to TIMP2 expression in non-tendon tissues.
paper.tldr: Two common variants in MMP3 and TIMP2 were associated with chronic Achilles tendinopathy in a large Han Chinese case-control sample. The effects are modest, and the authors call for replication before practical use.
paper.methods: Case-control design. Patients had at least 6 months of posterior lower-limb pain confirmed by ultrasound, and controls were unrelated healthy people from the same hospital. Twenty-one tag SNPs were genotyped on a Sequenom platform and analysed by logistic regression adjusted for BMI, with haplotype analysis, case-only epistasis tests, Bonferroni correction and GTEx eQTL look-ups.
paper.findings: After correction, rs679620 (MMP3) and rs4789932 (TIMP2) were significantly associated with chronic Achilles tendinopathy (P = 0.0006 and P = 0.0002). Epistasis analyses between the two genes were not significant, and rs4789932 was associated with TIMP2 expression in atrial appendage and tibial artery tissue.
paper.limitations: The odds ratios are modest, the sample is from one ethnic group and one hospital, there is no replication, and the authors note population stratification could not be adjusted with principal components. BMI was unbalanced between cases and controls, functional annotation suggested limited significance for both SNPs (rs679620 a 'tolerated' change, rs4789932 RegulomeDB score 4), the eQTL data come from healthy non-tendon tissues, and the authors state the results might differ in athlete cohorts.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that athletes carrying the implicated alleles may have higher risk, and they call for replication before practical use. On this study alone, genotype does not give a usable individual risk estimate.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should not use these variants to screen or rank athletes for tendon risk. The study does not change load or conditioning recommendations.
paper.rtp: The study does not inform return to sport or rehabilitation, since it compares chronic tendinopathy patients with controls and tests no treatment or recovery outcome.

records.sourceFile: Alpha-Actinin-3 deficiency might affect recovery from non-contact muscle injuries - Preliminary findings in a top level soccer team.pdf

paper.citation: Rodas G, Moreno-Pérez V, Del Coso J, Florit D, Osaba L, Lucia A. Alpha-Actinin-3 Deficiency Might Affect Recovery from Non-Contact Muscle Injuries: Preliminary Findings in a Top-Level Soccer Team. Genes. 2021;12:769.
paper.abstract: This study examined whether the ACTN3 R577X polymorphism (rs1815739) is associated with the risk of, and recovery time from, non-contact soft-tissue muscle injuries in 46 professional soccer players followed over five seasons. Genotype groups were compared for injury occurrence and return-to-play time. The authors report a trend toward more injuries in XX carriers and a significant association with longer return-to-play time, and they describe the findings as preliminary.
paper.tldr: In one professional club, players with the ACTN3 XX genotype had a trend toward more non-contact muscle injuries and longer return-to-play times. The group included only five XX players, so these results are a hypothesis and not a basis for genotype testing.
paper.methods: Cohort of 46 professional soccer players (22 men, 24 women) from one first-division club over five consecutive seasons (July 2015 to June 2020). Injuries were confirmed by ultrasound or MRI, and only non-contact lower-limb muscle injuries were analysed. Genotype was determined by KASP PCR, and groups were compared with chi-square tests and one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests. Ethics approval and written informed consent are reported.
paper.findings: Genotype frequencies were RR 41.3%, RX 47.8% and XX 10.9% (n = 5), with no demographic differences across genotypes. No XX player was injury-free over the study, compared with 31.6% of RR and 9.1% of RX players (p = 0.092), and the proportion with at least one injury was higher in X-allele carriers (RX plus XX) than in RR players (p = 0.033); among injured players, the number of injuries did not differ by genotype (p = 0.799). Mean return-to-play time was 20 +/- 10 days in RR, 17 +/- 12 in RX and 36 +/- 26 in XX players (p = 0.044), with the post hoc difference reported for XX versus RX only.
paper.limitations: The XX group has five players and the return-to-play SDs are large, so the estimates are imprecise, and the authors call the findings preliminary because of the small sample. The injury-risk result (p = 0.092) was not significant, and the study covers one club with only univariable tests; age, sex and position did not differ by genotype, but prior injury history and exposure were not accounted for. The overall return-to-play effect (p = 0.044) rests on a single pairwise difference, XX versus RX.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not use ACTN3 genotype to predict injury risk, clear a player, or set return-to-play timelines, because the authors say the evidence is too early for screening use. Genotype may be considered for research in larger cohorts that track injuries and recovery time with consistent medical records. Injury management should continue to follow standard imaging and clinical criteria.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not provide evidence for changing training or load based on ACTN3 genotype. Its relevance is as a hypothesis for future research on muscle injury and recovery, and it should not be used to individualise training plans.
paper.rtp: The study measured return-to-play time after non-contact muscle injury and found that the five XX players took longer on average than RX players. The authors describe this as preliminary and needing replication in larger cohorts, so it should not be used to set or extend return-to-play timelines; standard clinical criteria should guide clearance.

records.sourceFile: Alterations in hamstring properties of athletes with hamstring strain injuries can impact jump-landing performance.pdf

paper.citation: Jankaew A, Lin CF. Alterations in hamstring properties of athletes with hamstring strain injuries can impact jump-landing performance. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024;64.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared hamstring mechanical properties, flexibility and strength, and squat and countermovement jump mechanics in 16 athletes with a history of hamstring strain injury and 16 matched controls. The injured limb showed higher tone and stiffness, lower flexibility and strength, and poorer countermovement jump performance and landing mechanics than the control limb. The authors conclude that tissue property changes after strain may affect jump-landing performance.
paper.tldr: Male track and field athletes with a past hamstring strain had stiffer, less flexible and weaker hamstrings than uninjured controls, and they landed with higher forces in the countermovement jump. The study is small and cross-sectional, so it shows association rather than cause.
paper.methods: Single-session cross-sectional study of 16 male track and field athletes with a hamstring strain 3 to 24 months earlier and 16 matched controls without a history of hamstring strain. Tone, stiffness and elasticity were measured with MyotonPRO, flexibility with passive straight leg raise and active knee extension, and isometric strength at two angles. Squat and countermovement jumps were recorded on force plates. Groups were compared with one-way ANOVA and Bonferroni tests, and Pearson correlations were calculated. Reliability was moderate to high (ICC 0.929 for tone, 0.938 for stiffness, 0.652 for elasticity).
paper.findings: Injured limbs had higher tone (19.20 vs 18.07 Hz, P = 0.042) and stiffness (360.17 vs 327.56 N/m, P = 0.010) than control limbs. Active knee extension range was lower in injured limbs (54.56 vs 64.23 degrees, P = 0.002), and strength at 0 degrees was lower (207.99 vs 241.59 N, P = 0.040). In the countermovement jump, jump height was lower in the injured group (43.71 vs 48.53 cm, P = 0.037), and peak landing force and loading rate were higher than in controls. No squat jump differences were found between the injured and control legs, and no differences were found between the injured and non-injured legs of the injured athletes.
paper.limitations: Injury history was self-reported without imaging, all participants were men from one sport, the injured group was taller than controls (1.75 vs 1.71 m, P = 0.013), and the non-injured leg also differed from controls on active knee extension and CMJ landing force and loading rate, so the deficits are not clearly specific to the injured limb. The abstract says all hamstring properties correlated with jump-landing outcomes, but in Table IV passive straight leg raise correlated with no outcome and elasticity with only one (CMJ loading rate, r = 0.287), and the many correlations, apparently pooled across limbs, were not corrected for multiple comparisons. The discussion gives stiffness as 360.17 +/- 13.38 N/m, while Table II gives an SD of 31.88.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff assessing athletes after a hamstring strain could measure tone, stiffness, flexibility and strength alongside jump-landing tests, because these measures differed from controls. The authors recommend rehabilitation that addresses tissue properties through stretching, strengthening, neuromuscular retraining and gradual return to sport. This is a recommendation from the authors and was not tested in this design, so it should be checked against the athlete's own response.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Athletes with a past hamstring strain may show stiffer, weaker hamstrings and different landing forces in the countermovement jump, so jump and landing tests can be useful for monitoring change over time. The study cannot show that improving these measures will restore performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study supports including hamstring tone, stiffness, flexibility, strength and countermovement jump landing in assessments of athletes with prior hamstring strain. It does not test return-to-play criteria, and the authors note that athletes may return with persistent differences, so these measures should be used alongside standard clinical judgement.

records.sourceFile: Alterations in whole muscle quality and physiological cross-sectional area measured with quantitative MRI following ACL injury.pdf

paper.citation: Owen MK, Richardson L, Johnson DL, Vandsburger MH, Feiweier T, Thompson KL, et al. Alterations in whole muscle quality and physiological cross-sectional area measured with quantitative MRI following ACL injury. J Transl Med. 2025;23:79.
paper.abstract: This study used quantitative MRI, T1rho relaxation and diffusion tensor imaging, to compare muscle quality and physiological cross-sectional area (PCSA) of the quadriceps and hamstrings in the ACL-deficient and contralateral limbs of 10 participants imaged soon after a primary ACL tear and before reconstruction. The quadriceps showed longer T1rho times and smaller PCSA in the injured limb, while hamstring T1rho times were similar between limbs. The authors conclude that the thigh muscles respond differently to ACL injury before surgery.
paper.tldr: Within 5 to 35 days of an ACL tear, the injured limb had longer T1rho times in three quadriceps muscles and smaller PCSA in four thigh muscles compared with the uninjured limb. The sample is only 10 people, mostly women, so the quadriceps and hamstring contrast needs confirmation.
paper.methods: Analysis of a subset of a clinical trial (NCT03364647) in participants aged 14 to 40 with a primary ACL tear within 10 weeks and a Tegner activity level of at least 5; the authors call it a retrospective cohort (level 3) but all data come from one pre-surgical imaging session. T1rho and diffusion tensor MRI were acquired from both limbs before any pre-operative rehabilitation, and PCSA was calculated from muscle volume, fiber length and pennation angle. Limbs were compared with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with exploratory regression between T1rho and PCSA; 10 of 35 screened participants met the image-quality criteria.
paper.findings: T1rho was longer in the injured limb for the vastus lateralis (30.0 vs 27.9 ms, +7.0%, p = 0.02), rectus femoris (30.8 vs 26.4 ms, +15.4%, p = 0.01) and vastus intermedius (29.9 vs 27.1 ms, +9.4%, p < 0.01); vastus medialis (p = 0.06) and all hamstring T1rho values did not differ. PCSA was smaller in the injured limb for the vastus lateralis (-19.6%), vastus intermedius (-20.9%), vastus medialis (-26.0%, all p < 0.01) and semitendinosus (-15.0%, p = 0.03), while biceps femoris (+9.7%, p = 0.11) and semimembranosus did not differ significantly. In exploratory regressions, longer T1rho was associated with smaller PCSA in the vastus medialis (R2 = 0.54) and vastus intermedius (R2 = 0.49) but not the vastus lateralis.
paper.limitations: The sample is 10 people, 9 of them female, selected from 35 on image quality, and the contralateral limb is assumed to represent pre-injury status with no uninjured control group; the authors label the design both a retrospective cohort and cross-sectional. The discussion says T1rho and PCSA were altered in all quadriceps muscles, but vastus medialis T1rho was not significant (p = 0.06) and rectus femoris PCSA was not measured (its volume did not differ between limbs). The abstract conclusion that the hamstrings were unaffected conflicts with the significant semitendinosus PCSA reduction, and the regressions were exploratory with n = 10.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians should not assume the hamstrings are unaffected after an ACL tear, because semitendinosus PCSA was smaller in this sample. The quadriceps findings support the idea that quadriceps muscle changes are present before reconstruction, which may matter for pre-operative planning. The authors' suggestion of pre-surgical quadriceps strengthening was not tested in this study and should be treated as a hypothesis.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Quadriceps and hamstring size and quality may already differ between limbs in the first weeks after an ACL tear, so strength and size asymmetries are worth tracking during rehabilitation. This study does not show that training changes these MRI measures or improves performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study describes pre-surgical muscle changes in the first 5 to 35 days after injury, which may be relevant to later quadriceps strength deficits. It does not measure strength, function or return-to-sport outcomes, and it cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria.

records.sourceFile: Altered gut microbiota richness in individuals with a history of lateral ankle sprain.pdf

paper.citation: Terada M, Uchida M, Suga T, Isaka T. Altered gut microbiota richness in individuals with a history of lateral ankle sprain. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This study compared gut microbiota diversity in 50 male collegiate athletes with (n = 32) and without (n = 18) a history of lateral ankle sprain. Faecal samples were collected during the off-season and analysed by 16S rRNA sequencing. The sprain group had lower Chao1 and ACE richness and a higher proportion of Bacteroides fragilis and Ruminococcus gnavus, with no difference in overall community composition. The authors suggest a possible link between lateral ankle sprain and gut microbiota richness.
paper.tldr: Male college athletes with a past ankle sprain had fewer gut bacterial species than athletes without one, along with a higher share of two bacteria. Because the study is cross-sectional with no diet control, it shows an association only.
paper.methods: Case-control design, described by the authors as single-blinded, drawn from 142 male athletes in basketball, American football and track and field; after excluding 92 with other musculoskeletal injury histories, 32 with a previous lateral ankle sprain and 18 controls remained. One morning faecal sample was collected per athlete in the off-season and analysed by 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing with QIIME and Greengenes. Alpha diversity was compared with independent t-tests and beta diversity with unweighted UniFrac and Euclidean distances; diet was not monitored and no a priori sample size calculation was made.
paper.findings: Observed OTUs were lower in the sprain group (430.35 vs 849.11, P < 0.001, d = -1.05), as were Chao1 (2227.62 vs 2899.39, P = 0.020) and ACE (2234.14 vs 3001.41, P = 0.035). Shannon and Simpson indices did not differ. Bacteroides fragilis (2.67% vs 0.72%, P = 0.024) and Ruminococcus gnavus (1.45% vs 0.35%, P = 0.021) were higher in the sprain group. Overall beta diversity did not differ between groups (R2 = 0.01, P = 0.414).
paper.limitations: The authors call the design both case-control and cross-sectional, so causation cannot be inferred, and diet, inflammation and psychological state were not measured in this sample of 50 men from three sports with no a priori sample size calculation. The text gives beta-diversity P = 0.414 while the Figure 1 legend gives P = 0.53, the reported overall mean of 787.40 OTUs does not match the group means (430 and 849), and the 95% confidence intervals for the Bacteroides fragilis and Ruminococcus gnavus effect sizes include zero despite P values below 0.05. The authors suggest the richness differences may be clinically meaningful and propose microbiome measures as possible biomarkers, which the study does not test.
paper.practicalImplications: Gut microbiota measures are not ready for use in managing ankle sprains, so staff should not use these results to screen athletes, judge recovery or select treatments. The authors themselves describe the biomarker and treatment ideas as speculative and call for prospective studies and clinical intervention trials, so research teams could repeat the comparison with diet and inflammatory markers recorded.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study does not show that gut microbiota affects training response or performance, and it provides no basis for changing training or nutrition plans for athletes with a previous ankle sprain.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It does not measure ankle function, symptoms, or readiness to play, and the authors do not link the microbiome findings to recovery status.

records.sourceFile: American Medical Society for Sports Medicine position statement on concussion in sport.pdf

paper.citation: Harmon KG, Clugston JR, Dec K, Hainline B, Herring S, Kane SF, et al. American Medical Society for Sports Medicine position statement on concussion in sport. Br J Sports Med. 2019;53:213-225.
paper.abstract: This position statement from the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine updates its 2013 statement on sport-related concussion. It covers the definition, pathophysiology, epidemiology, diagnosis, sideline and office assessment, biomarkers and imaging, management of acute and persistent symptoms, return to learn and return to sport, long-term risks, prevention and future research. Recommendations are graded with the Strength of Recommendation Taxonomy.
paper.tldr: Concussion is still diagnosed clinically, and no objective test, biomarker, impact sensor or genetic test is validated for diagnosis. Athletes should be removed from play when concussion is suspected, and return to sport should follow a stepwise progression with at least 24 hours without symptoms at each stage.
paper.methods: Position statement written by a writing group selected by the AMSSM board, with conference calls, an in-person meeting and iterative drafts. Systematic reviews were used as primary literature sources when available. Recommendations are graded A (consistent good-quality patient-oriented evidence), B (inconsistent or limited evidence) or C (consensus, expert opinion, usual practice or case series). No formal search protocol or quality appraisal of the whole literature is described.
paper.findings: Symptoms are the most sensitive indicator of concussion; the statement describes the SCAT5 and Child SCAT5 as the Concussion in Sport Group's recommended sideline tools, notes there are no sensitivity and specificity studies of these versions, and says test-retest reliability of commonly used sideline tests is below the accepted threshold for clinical use. Impact monitors and fluid biomarkers currently have no role in diagnosis or management, and there is no scientific support for genetic testing (all grade B). About 80 to 90% of concussed older adolescents and adults return to preinjury function within 2 weeks and younger athletes within 4 weeks; symptom-limited activity may begin after 24 to 48 hours of relative rest, and a stepwise return to sport is recommended with each stage at least 24 hours without symptoms for young athletes. Continuing to play immediately after a concussion is a risk for greater symptom burden and prolonged recovery, and returning before full recovery raises the risk of repeat concussion.
paper.limitations: The statement says that definitive outcome-based data are absent, many recommendations are graded C, and the authors describe the return-to-sport progression as empiric, without evidence for its sequence or stage duration. All studies in the sideline test table (Table 3) were rated high risk of bias except one (Fuller et al.), and the statement notes that concussion rates in Table 2 are hard to compare because denominators vary. No systematic literature search or formal grading of the whole evidence base is reported beyond using systematic reviews where available.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should evaluate any suspected concussion at the time of injury, remove the athlete from play and follow up with serial assessment, because no single test confirms the diagnosis. Use symptom checklists and multimodal assessment rather than impact sensors, biomarkers or genetic testing to make diagnostic or return-to-play decisions. Plan a stepwise return to play with at least 24 hours without symptoms per stage, and do not reintroduce contact until the progression reaches the contact stages and the athlete shows psychological readiness.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: After a concussion, training should be rebuilt through the staged progression of symptom-limited activity, light aerobic work, sport-specific drills, non-contact training, full practice and then competition, rather than returned to full load. The statement does not address performance measurement after concussion.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Concussion-related symptoms and signs should be resolved before return to sport, and a six-stage progression with at least 24 hours without symptoms per stage is recommended for young athletes. The statement also advises a return-to-learn plan before return to sport training for student-athletes, and says that individual factors such as age, prior concussion and level of play should shape the progression.

records.sourceFile: Anterior cruciate ligament injury occurrence, return to sport and subsequent injury in the Australian High Performance Sports System - A 5-year retrospective analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Rigg JD, Panagodage Perera NK, Toohey LA, Cooke J, Hughes D. Anterior cruciate ligament injury occurrence, return to sport and subsequent injury in the Australian High Performance Sports System: A 5-year retrospective analysis. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2023;64:140-146.
paper.abstract: Retrospective case series of ACL injuries recorded in the Australian High Performance Sport System from 2015 to May 2020. Of 132 ACL injuries in 108 athletes, 25.8% were subsequent ACL injuries and the median return-to-sport time was 369 days, with shorter times in older athletes.
paper.tldr: In this high-performance system, ACL injuries took about a year to return to sport, and about one in four ACL injuries were repeat injuries. Older athletes returned sooner, and concurrent knee injuries did not significantly lengthen return time in this series.
paper.methods: Retrospective case series using injury records entered prospectively into the Athlete Management System (Smartabase) and coded with OSICS-10.1. Return to sport was the date the treating practitioner cleared full training and competition. Return times were compared with Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests and sex proportions with chi-squared tests; cases without completed return were right censored.
paper.findings: ACL injuries were 6.4% of 2,071 knee injuries, and the proportion was higher in female than male athletes (7.6% vs 4.7%, p=0.011). Median return-to-sport time was 369 days (102 records with return data) and differed across four age groups (p=0.008), from 487 days under 18 to 318 days over 25. Male and female return times did not differ significantly (311 vs 373 days, p=0.297), and concurrent knee pathology did not significantly lengthen return time (402 vs 365 days, p=0.549). Of 108 athletes, 26 (24.1%, Table 1) had a subsequent ACL injury, and subsequent injuries made up 25.8% of ACL injuries, though for 10 of these the initial injury predated the surveillance period. Netball (29.5%), winter sports (15.9%) and basketball (12.2%) had the most injuries, and 48.5% occurred in training.
paper.limitations: Retrospective design with no exposure data, so no incidence rates or sport or sex risk comparisons. Not all athletes were followed to return, and surgical versus conservative management was not recorded. The text gives 6 contralateral subsequent injuries but Table 2 gives 8, and the Discussion gives 16.7% of athletes with a subsequent injury while Table 1 gives 24.1%; the table values are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan return-to-sport timelines for high-performance athletes around about a year of time loss (median 369 days), expecting longer timelines in younger athletes. The authors recommend primary prevention aimed at female and younger athletes and tertiary prevention against repeat injury, since about a quarter of ACL injuries here were subsequent. Concurrent meniscal or cartilage injury did not significantly lengthen return time in this series.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the sport counts (netball, winter sports, basketball) and the May peak to direct ACL prevention work to the squads with the most injuries. Exposure data were not available, so the counts do not show which sports carry the highest risk per athlete exposure.
paper.rtp: This series supports planning for about 12 months of time loss after ACL injury, with shorter times in older athletes, and it flags a high repeat-injury rate. It does not give criteria for clearing an athlete to return, because return was defined as clearance by the treating practitioner.

records.sourceFile: Anterior pelvic tilt increases hamstring strain and is a key factor to target for injury prevention and rehabilitation.pdf

paper.citation: Mendiguchia J, Garrues MA, Schilders E, Myer GD, Dalmau-Pastor M. Anterior pelvic tilt increases hamstring strain and is a key factor to target for injury prevention and rehabilitation. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2024;32:573-582.
paper.abstract: In vitro cadaver study of seven fresh-frozen lower limbs in which anterior pelvic tilt from 0 to 25 degrees produced significant, non-uniform hamstring elongation. Elongation was greater in the proximal than the distal hamstring region, and the authors propose pelvic position as a hamstring strain regulator.
paper.tldr: In fixed cadaver specimens, tilting the pelvis forward lengthened all three hamstring muscles, with the greatest lengthening near the ischial tuberosity. This supports pelvic position as a factor for hamstring work, but it has not been tested in athletes.
paper.methods: Seven fresh-frozen lower limbs with pelvis and lumbar spine were fixed to a custom bench. Nine markers were placed in the hamstrings, and anterior pelvic tilt was set at six angles (0 to 25 degrees in 5-degree steps) with hip at 30 degrees and knee at 20 degrees flexion. Muscle lengths were measured with 3D stereoscopic reconstruction and compared with paired t-tests (p<0.05).
paper.findings: Each increase in anterior pelvic tilt lengthened all three hamstring muscles (semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris long head). Proximal regions lengthened more than the distal region (over 1 cm per 5 degrees vs about 0.4 cm per 5 degrees). At the proximal region the semimembranosus free tendon showed significantly greater length change than the conjoint tendon, while differences between muscles at the distal region were not significant.
paper.limitations: Only seven specimens were used, which the authors acknowledge, although results were consistent across specimens. There was no muscle contraction or fatigue, the femur and tibia were fixed, and the study did not test pelvis and hip or knee motion together as in sprinting.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians managing proximal hamstring problems could assess pelvic tilt, as the authors suggest, because the study links tilt to proximal hamstring lengthening. Exercise choices for hamstring work could consider pelvic position, but the study does not show that changing tilt changes injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: Strength and conditioning staff can consider pelvic position when programming hamstring exercises, as the authors suggest, but this rests on cadaver data. The study does not show that changing pelvic tilt reduces hamstring strain during sprinting.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport: it measured passive lengthening in cadavers, not strain, rehabilitation outcomes or re-injury. Its only rehabilitation implication is the authors' suggestion to consider pelvic position for proximal hamstring injuries.

records.sourceFile: Antidoping testing and testicle cancer diagnosis - An unexpected helper.pdf

paper.citation: Vecchiato M, Baioccato V, Palermi S. Antidoping testing and testicle cancer diagnosis: An unexpected helper. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: Short communication on testicular cancer detected incidentally through routine anti-doping tests in elite male athletes, since hCG is prohibited in men and can be produced by testicular tumors. The authors compiled publicly reported cases from 2010 onward to show how early detection allowed treatment and return to sport.
paper.tldr: An elevated hCG result on a male athlete's doping test can be the first sign of testicular cancer, and 13 publicly reported athletes were diagnosed this way since 2010. Most were treated early and returned to competition, so a positive hCG finding should prompt prompt medical evaluation.
paper.methods: Systematic web-based search using Google Advanced Search with keywords listed in a supplementary table. Cases were included only when a positive hCG doping test in a male athlete was clearly linked to a testicular cancer diagnosis; cases not resulting from a doping control were excluded. Case details came from publicly available reports.
paper.findings: Thirteen athletes (ages 17 to 34; football, baseball, beach volleyball, athletics, ice hockey, swimming, cycling and basketball) were diagnosed after a positive test between 2010 and 2023. Treatments ranged from surgery alone to surgery with chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and most returned to competition, in several cases within months. One 17-year-old footballer had metastatic disease and died in 2014, and one case was a recurrence detected through testing.
paper.limitations: Evidence comes from press and public reports without clinical verification, and the list is limited to publicly identified athletes. The text states return to play was complete in all cases, yet the table records one athlete who died of metastatic disease after a brief return; the table details are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical staff should treat an elevated hCG finding in a male athlete as a possible sign of testicular cancer and arrange prompt specialist evaluation, history, examination, laboratory tests and imaging, as WADA guidance requires a pathological cause to be excluded. The paper does not support routine cancer screening through doping tests.
paper.athleteDev: This paper has no training or performance application. Its relevance for performance staff is awareness that an hCG finding may reflect illness rather than doping.
paper.rtp: Reported cases show that athletes diagnosed early often returned to competition after surgery, with or without chemotherapy, but timelines came from press reports and varied from weeks to over a year. The paper gives no clinical criteria for return to sport after testicular cancer.

records.sourceFile: Applying personal genetic data to      injury risk assessment in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Goodlin GT, Roos AK, Roos TR, Hawkins C, Beache S, Baur S, et al. Applying Personal Genetic Data to Injury Risk Assessment in Athletes. PLoS ONE. 2015;10(4):e0122676.
paper.abstract: Published genetic association studies of health and disease were mined for 124 SNPs linked to sports-related injury and trait categories, and 91% had not been used in sports genetics before. Fourteen triathletes were genotyped and counselled, and most were favourable about the program and acted on their results.
paper.tldr: A pilot in 14 collegiate triathletes used genetic data from health studies to give individual injury and nutrition advice. Most athletes who were advised to change training acted on the advice, but there was no control group, so the program's effect on injury cannot be judged from this study.
paper.methods: Genetic association studies (GWAS catalogue and candidate-gene studies) were searched for six categories relevant to athletes, and SNPs were selected from genome-wide significant or candidate-gene reports. Fourteen Stanford triathletes were genotyped through 23andMe, received an hour-long consultation on their risk profile, and completed surveys at 3 and 12 months (10 and 13 responses).
paper.findings: The literature search identified 124 SNPs across six categories, of which 113 had not previously been used in sports genetics. Twelve of the 14 athletes were recommended training interventions, and 8 of those 12 reported acting on the results at follow-up. The proportion of athletes injured was 71% (10 of 14) in the year before the study and 33% (4 of 12 with full data) in the follow-up year, but no comparison group was studied.
paper.limitations: The authors state that 14 athletes is too few for a rigorous trial and that the program's effect on injury could not be tested. The risk estimates come mostly from studies in other populations, and the ACL and Achilles associations rest on small candidate-gene studies. Survey response fell from 14 to 10 at 3 months, and the injury figures are self-reported across two different periods.
paper.practicalImplications: In this pilot, genetic results led some athletes to change training or diet, such as eccentric calf work and softer running surfaces for Achilles risk, and an endurance athlete with magnesium risk moved to a drink with more magnesium and potassium. The authors judge the genetic associations to add only a small amount to overall injury risk and consider genetic testing premature for the general athletic population.
paper.athleteDev: In this pilot, genetic results prompted changes such as eccentric calf strengthening and softer running surfaces for three athletes with Achilles risk, and a higher-magnesium electrolyte drink for one athlete with magnesium-deficiency risk. The authors note triathletes can shift running volume to cycling or swimming when predisposed to running injuries, but the study did not test whether any of these changes improved performance or reduced injury.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not test injured athletes, rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions, and its only injury-related actions were preventive changes such as calf strengthening.

records.sourceFile: Are EPB41 and alpha-synuclein diagnostic biomarkers of sport related concussion - Findings from the NCAA DoD CARE Consortium.pdf

paper.citation: Vorn R, Devoto C, Meier TB, Lai C, Yun S, Broglio SP, et al. Are EPB41 and alpha-synuclein diagnostic biomarkers of sport-related concussion? Findings from the NCAA and Department of Defense CARE Consortium. Journal of Sport and Health Science. 2022.
paper.abstract: In a multicentre case-control study of 140 concussed and 21 non-concussed collegiate athletes, plasma proteomic profiling identified 338 differentially abundant proteins. The top 20 discriminated concussed from non-concussed athletes with an AUC of 0.954, and EPB41 and SNCA together had an AUC of 1.000 in samples taken 7-48 h after injury.
paper.tldr: In a 140-athlete case-control study, plasma EPB41 and SNCA separated concussed from non-concussed athletes when blood was drawn 7-48 h after injury. The result is an exploratory candidate from 21 controls with no independent validation, so it is not yet a test staff can use.
paper.methods: Prospective multicentre case-control study within the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium, 2015-2019. Plasma from concussed athletes (n = 140, collected within 48 h) and matched non-concussed controls (n = 21) was analysed with the SOMAscan aptamer assay for 1305 proteins. Proteins were compared with Mann-Whitney, chi-square or Kruskal-Wallis tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and the top 20 were modelled with logistic regression and ROC analysis.
paper.findings: Across 0-48 h, 338 proteins differed between groups (319 higher and 19 lower in concussed athletes). The top 20 proteins gave an AUC of 0.954 (95% CI 0.923-0.986), and the SCAT-3 symptom score gave 0.939, with BESS (0.681) and SAC (0.697) lower. In the 7-48 h subgroup (n = 75) EPB41 had an AUC of 0.956 (95% CI 0.902-1.000), SNCA 0.875 (95% CI 0.794-0.957) and the pair 1.000; the 0-6 h subgroup (n = 65) had 66 differing proteins that were not significant after correction and was not tested for discrimination.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, with 21 controls, mostly White non-Hispanic men in contact sports, and controls had no prior concussions while 45% of cases had at least one (p = 0.004). Blood draw timing ranged from 0 to 48 h, controls may include unreported concussions, and the top-20 proteins were selected and tested in the same samples with no independent validation, so the perfect AUC is likely optimistic. This is an accepted pre-proof; the subgroup labels ('6 h post-injury' for 0-6 h, 'after 6 h' for 7-48 h) are easy to misread, and minor numbers differ between sections (0-48 h CI lower bound 0.922 vs 0.923; SCAT-3 AUC 0.939 vs 0.938).
paper.practicalImplications: The authors present EPB41 and SNCA as candidate diagnostic markers that need validation in larger cohorts, with accuracy they describe as comparable to SCAT-3 symptom scores. The paper does not support using these proteins in place of clinical assessment or in any diagnostic or clearance decision.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not address training or performance, since its outcome is diagnostic accuracy for concussion. The protein levels should not be read as a readiness, fatigue or training-load measure.
paper.rtp: The study does not support return-to-play decisions. It compared concussed and non-concussed athletes within 48 h of injury and did not measure whether protein levels track recovery or clearance, which the authors say needs prognostic study first.

records.sourceFile: Are rugby league players involved in more tackles than normal prior to an injury sustained during a tackle event (1).pdf

paper.citation: Hopkinson M, Nicholson G, Rennie G, Sawczuk T, Owen C, Hendricks S, et al. Are rugby league players involved in more tackles than normal, prior to an injury sustained during a tackle event? Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022;40(22):2517-2523.
paper.abstract: Video analysis of 61 tackle-related injuries in male rugby league players compared tackle counts in the 10 minutes before injury with matched uninjured periods. Injured players made fewer tackles across the 10 minutes but more in the final minute before the injurious tackle.
paper.tldr: In 61 rugby league players injured in a tackle, the 10 minutes before injury contained fewer tackles than usual, but the final minute contained more. The finding is a small observational association and does not show that tackle load caused the injury.
paper.methods: Matched case-control observational study using video analysis of 61 tackle-related injuries from the 2017 and 2018 Super League seasons (41 ball carriers and 20 tacklers). Tackles in the 10 minutes before each injurious tackle were coded in 1-minute blocks, and matched control periods came from the same player when uninjured, taken from OptaRugby data. Generalised linear mixed models with a Poisson distribution were used, with a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.006.
paper.findings: Injured players were involved in fewer tackles over the 10-minute window (2.1, 95% CI 1.7-2.6) than in their uninjured periods (2.6, 95% CI 2.2-3.0), OR 0.8 (0.7-1.0, P = 0.02). In the final minute before the injurious tackle they were involved in more tackles (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.3-2.8, P = 0.001), the only result the authors report as significant after Bonferroni adjustment (P < 0.006); the rise from minute 1-2 to minute 0-1 (OR 2.4, P = 0.011) did not meet that threshold. Forwards showed more final-minute tackles than uninjured forwards (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-3.0, P = 0.01); the back result is printed as OR 3.2 with a 95% CI of 0.5-1.0, which cannot be correct.
paper.limitations: The sample is small (61 injuries from one league over two seasons) after inclusion criteria removed 123 injuries, and only injuries where the player left the field immediately were kept. The control count is 1,280 in the abstract but 1,220 in the methods; the back-player OR (3.2, CI 0.5-1.0) is impossible, the tackler vs ball-carrier ORs of 0.2 are described as tacklers having more tackles, and the tackler final-minute OR of 2.8 has a CI (0.9-8.1) that includes 1. Fatigue was not measured, and 10 of 61 injured players (16%) were involved in no tackle in the 10-minute window.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest the final minute before an injurious tackle needs closer study, alongside tackle technique and tackle density. Staff could review the final minute of tackle activity when investigating tackle-related injuries, but the study does not set a tackle limit or a threshold for substitution.
paper.athleteDev: The association was with tackle involvement in the final minute before injury, not the 10-minute total, which the authors suggest may reflect transient fatigue. Fatigue was not measured and most subgroup results did not survive correction, so the study does not set match or training tackle thresholds.
paper.rtp: The study addresses tackle-related injury risk, not return to play. It includes only players who were injured, and it does not assess return-to-play timing or readiness to resume tackling.
